title: Inky Cap Mushroom and Alcohol: Why It Causes a Toxic Reaction
excerpt: Why the inky cap mushroom makes you sick if you drink: how coprine blocks acetaldehyde clearance, the symptoms, how long to wait, shaggy mane safety, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Why inky cap mushrooms react with alcohol: how coprine blocks acetaldehyde, the symptoms, how long to wait before drinking, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the common inky cap mushroom (*Coprinopsis atramentaria*, long known as *Coprinus atramentarius*) is edible on its own, but if you drink alcohol within roughly three days of eating it, you can get a sudden, unpleasant reaction: a hot red face and neck, a racing or pounding heart, nausea, vomiting, sweating, and a throbbing headache. It happens because a compound in the mushroom, called **coprine**, blocks the enzyme your body uses to clear acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol. It's the same basic chemistry as the alcohol-deterrent drug disulfiram (Antabuse). The reaction is usually short-lived and rarely dangerous for healthy adults, but it can be frightening and hard on anyone with heart problems.

**The quick rules:** If you've eaten inky caps, or any wild mushroom you're not completely sure about, skip alcohol for at least 72 hours, and many foragers wait five days to be safe. Don't drink in the hours before an inky cap meal either. If you're reacting right now, stop drinking, sit or lie down, sip water, and call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) for advice. Call 911 if you have chest pain, fainting, trouble breathing, or confusion.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research on mushroom toxins and alcohol. It is not a substitute for a doctor, pharmacist, or poison center. **Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) or see a doctor if** you've eaten a wild mushroom and then had any alcohol and feel unwell, you aren't sure what species you ate, symptoms started more than a few hours after eating the mushroom (which can point to a different, more dangerous mushroom), or you have heart disease, high or low blood pressure, or take heart or blood pressure medicine. **Call 911 for** chest pain, fainting, a very fast or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, trouble breathing, or confusion.

## What Is the Inky Cap Mushroom?

"Inky cap" (or "ink cap") is a loose name for several mushrooms whose caps dissolve into a black, ink-like liquid as they age. That self-digesting process is called deliquescence, and it's how the group got its name. In the past, the black liquid was actually used as writing ink.

The species that matters for alcohol is the **common inky cap**, *Coprinopsis atramentaria*. You'll still see it listed under its older name, *Coprinus atramentarius*, in many field guides. It has a nickname that tells you everything: **tippler's bane**.

Here's how foragers usually describe it:

- **Cap:** gray to gray-brown, bell- or egg-shaped when young, often with fine grooves or a slightly scaly top, usually a few centimeters across.
- **Gills:** crowded, starting white or pale gray and turning black and inky from the edge inward as the mushroom matures.
- **Habit:** grows in clusters, often from buried wood, old stumps, lawns, gardens, and disturbed ground, especially after rain in spring and autumn.
- **Life span:** short. Caps can start dissolving within a day of appearing, so they need to be picked young and cooked quickly.

The mushroom is widespread across North America, Europe, and other temperate regions, which is why reactions turn up fairly regularly in poison center reports, usually in people who cooked a batch from their yard and then had a beer or a glass of wine with dinner.

> **A note on identification:** this article is not a foraging guide. Several mushrooms look broadly similar to inky caps when young, and some toxic species can be mistaken for edible ones by beginners. Never eat a wild mushroom unless an experienced local expert has confirmed the species in person.

## Why Inky Caps and Alcohol Don't Mix: The Coprine Mechanism

To understand the reaction, it helps to know how your body normally handles alcohol. It happens in two steps, mostly in the liver:

1. **Alcohol becomes acetaldehyde.** An enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) turns ethanol into **acetaldehyde**. Acetaldehyde is the genuinely nasty part of drinking. It's toxic, it widens blood vessels, and it's linked to flushing, nausea, and a pounding heart. (Our explainer on [what acetaldehyde is](/never-hungover/what-is-acetaldehyde) goes deeper.)
2. **Acetaldehyde becomes acetate.** A second enzyme, **aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH)**, quickly turns acetaldehyde into acetate, a harmless substance your body breaks down into carbon dioxide and water.

In a normal night of drinking, step two keeps up well enough that acetaldehyde never builds up much. Coprine breaks step two.

### What coprine does

The inky cap contains an unusual amino acid called **coprine**. Coprine itself is fairly inactive. Once you eat it, your body converts it into a compound called **1-aminocyclopropanol**, and that's the molecule that does the damage. It binds to aldehyde dehydrogenase and switches it off.

With ALDH blocked, step one keeps running but step two stalls. Every drink you have keeps producing acetaldehyde, and it has nowhere to go. Blood acetaldehyde rises to many times its normal level, and you feel it within minutes.

### Why the mushroom alone is fine

Here's the strange part. If you eat inky caps and drink nothing, you usually feel completely normal. Blocking ALDH only matters when there's acetaldehyde to clear, and acetaldehyde only comes from alcohol (in any meaningful amount). So the mushroom is a perfectly good meal on its own. The trouble appears only when alcohol enters the picture.

### Why the risk lasts for days

The enzyme block isn't a quick on-off switch. The active compound binds to ALDH in a way that keeps the enzyme out of action until your body makes fresh enzyme to replace it. That takes time. This is why a drink two days after the meal can still trigger a reaction. Toxicology references generally put the risk window at about **72 hours**, and some reports describe reactions a little beyond that, which is why cautious foragers wait up to five days.

## Symptoms of an Inky Cap and Alcohol Reaction

The reaction is often called a **coprine syndrome** or a **disulfiram-like reaction**. It tends to start quickly, usually within about 5 to 30 minutes of drinking, though it can take up to a couple of hours. Common symptoms include:

- **Flushing:** the face, neck, and upper chest turn red and feel hot. This is often the first and most obvious sign.
- **Racing or pounding heart:** a fast heartbeat (tachycardia) and palpitations, sometimes with a feeling of anxiety or dread.
- **Nausea and vomiting.**
- **Throbbing headache**, often felt in the temples or neck.
- **Sweating** and feeling flushed and clammy at the same time.
- **Tingling** or numbness in the hands, feet, or face.
- **A metallic taste** in the mouth.
- **Dizziness or lightheadedness**, especially when standing, because blood pressure can drop.
- **Shortness of breath** or a tight chest in some people.

Most reactions fade within a few hours as the body slowly works through the acetaldehyde. But here's the catch: **if you drink again before the enzyme recovers, the reaction can come back.** That's why people sometimes report several episodes over a weekend, each time they had another drink.

### How serious is it?

For most healthy adults, the coprine reaction is miserable but not life-threatening, and toxicology sources describe it as typically self-limiting, meaning it resolves on its own. The real risks are:

- **Low blood pressure and fainting**, which can lead to falls and injuries.
- **Strain on the heart**, which matters for anyone with heart disease, an irregular rhythm, or high blood pressure.
- **Dehydration** from repeated vomiting.
- **Confusion about what's happening.** If you don't know about the mushroom-alcohol link, sudden flushing and a pounding heart can feel like an allergic reaction or a heart attack, and you might take the wrong steps.

The amount of alcohol matters. A few sips may cause only mild flushing, while several drinks on top of a large inky cap meal can produce a much stronger reaction.

## When to See a Doctor or Call for Help

> **Get help now.** Call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) if you're reacting after eating a wild mushroom and drinking, even if it seems mild, so a specialist can advise you. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if you have:** chest pain or pressure; fainting or nearly fainting; a heartbeat that's very fast, irregular, or won't slow down; trouble breathing; vomiting you can't stop; or confusion. Also seek care if you have a heart condition or take blood pressure medicine, since a drop in blood pressure can hit harder.
>
> **Be especially careful if symptoms started six or more hours after eating the mushroom**, whether or not you drank. Coprine reactions are tied to drinking and come on fast. Severe stomach symptoms that begin many hours after a wild mushroom meal are a classic warning sign of the deadly amatoxin mushrooms (such as death caps), which can destroy the liver. That's a medical emergency even if you start to feel better.

If possible, bring a sample of the mushroom (or a photo, and any leftovers) with you. It helps doctors and poison specialists confirm what you ate.

## What to Do If You're Having a Reaction Right Now

If you've realized you drank after eating inky caps and you're starting to flush:

1. **Stop drinking immediately.** Every additional sip adds more acetaldehyde.
2. **Sit or lie down.** If you feel dizzy, lie down with your legs slightly raised to help your blood pressure. Get up slowly.
3. **Sip water** to stay hydrated, especially if you're vomiting.
4. **Stay with someone** who can call for help if things get worse.
5. **Call Poison Control** (1-800-222-1222 in the US) for advice. They handle mushroom questions all the time and can tell you whether you need to be seen.
6. **Don't drink again for several days.** Plan on at least 72 hours from your last inky cap meal, and longer to be safe.

In the hospital, treatment is supportive, which means treating the symptoms: IV fluids for low blood pressure or dehydration, anti-nausea medicine, and heart monitoring if needed. There's no special home remedy that clears acetaldehyde faster, and you shouldn't try to "sweat it out" with exercise or a hot shower, since both can drop your blood pressure further.

## How Long After Eating Inky Caps Can You Drink?

This is the question most people actually search for, so here's a clear answer.

- **Before the meal:** avoid alcohol for several hours beforehand. If alcohol is still in your system when the coprine takes effect, you can react.
- **After the meal:** wait at least **72 hours** (three days) before drinking. Some foragers and mushroom clubs recommend **five days** because reactions have been reported a little past the three-day mark.
- **Repeated meals:** if you eat inky caps over several days, count the waiting period from your **last** meal.
- **Cooking doesn't help:** coprine is not destroyed by normal cooking, so a well-cooked dish carries the same risk as a lightly cooked one.

Also watch out for hidden alcohol. Wine-based sauces, beer batter, liqueur desserts, some cough syrups, and some mouthwashes contain alcohol. Small amounts are less likely to cause a strong reaction than a full drink, but if you've just eaten inky caps, it's simplest to avoid them for a few days too.

## Shaggy Mane and Alcohol: Is the Shaggy Ink Cap Safe?

The **shaggy mane**, or shaggy ink cap (*Coprinus comatus*), is the inky cap that foragers most often actually eat. It's tall and white with shaggy scales on its cap, and it also dissolves into black ink as it ages.

The good news: the shaggy mane is generally considered **not** to contain coprine, and most field guides list it as safe to eat with alcohol. The species were once grouped together under the same genus, *Coprinus*, which is part of why the confusion persists. Genetic studies later split them, and the common inky cap moved to *Coprinopsis*.

There are a few caveats worth knowing:

- **Occasional reports exist.** A small number of people have reported mild symptoms after eating shaggy manes with alcohol. It isn't clear whether these were true reactions, a mix-up with another species, or something else, such as a stomach upset from rich food and drink. There is no good evidence that shaggy manes cause the coprine reaction, but some cautious foragers skip alcohol anyway.
- **Misidentification is the bigger risk.** Young common inky caps and shaggy manes can grow in similar places. If someone picks a mixed batch, the common inky caps in it can cause a full reaction.
- **Pick them young.** Shaggy manes are only good to eat when they're fresh and white. Once the gills blacken, they're past it.

If you're not completely sure which inky cap you have, treat it as the common inky cap and skip alcohol for at least three days.

## Other Mushrooms That React With Alcohol

The common inky cap is the best-known example, but it isn't the only one. Toxicology literature mentions a few other mushrooms that have been associated with disulfiram-like reactions when eaten with alcohol, such as the **club-footed funnel** (*Ampulloclitocybe clavipes*, formerly *Clitocybe clavipes*). For some other species, the reports are older, scattered, or disputed.

The practical rule is simple: **if you're eating any wild mushroom for the first time, don't drink alcohol with it.** That way, if you do have a reaction, you know it isn't the alcohol. And if you have a stomach reaction, you and your doctor won't have to untangle two possible causes.

Cultivated mushrooms from the grocery store, like button, cremini, portobello, shiitake, and oyster mushrooms, are not known to cause this reaction. Supplements made from functional mushrooms are a separate topic; we cover them in our guide to [functional mushrooms and alcohol](/never-hungover/functional-mushrooms-and-alcohol).

## Coprine, Disulfiram, and Other Drugs That Cause the Same Reaction

The inky cap reaction is a classic teaching example in pharmacology because it shows exactly what happens when acetaldehyde can't be cleared. Several other things cause a similar reaction through the same or a related route:

| Cause | How it blocks acetaldehyde clearance | How long the risk lasts |
|---|---|---|
| Common inky cap (coprine) | Its breakdown product switches off aldehyde dehydrogenase | About 3 days, sometimes longer |
| Disulfiram (Antabuse) | Prescription drug that irreversibly blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase | Up to about 2 weeks after the last dose |
| Some antibiotics and antifungals | Some are thought to interfere with alcohol metabolism; the strength of the evidence varies by drug | Varies; follow the label and pharmacist advice |
| The ALDH2 gene variant ("Asian flush") | An inherited, less active form of the enzyme | Lifelong |

**Disulfiram** is the best-known relative. It was discovered by accident in the 1940s, when researchers in Denmark who were taking it noticed they became sick after drinking. It's prescribed to support people who have chosen not to drink, because the reaction makes alcohol deeply unpleasant. Coprine was even studied as a possible alternative to disulfiram, but research didn't move forward, partly because of toxicity concerns in animal studies.

**Antibiotics** are a common source of confusion. The antibiotic metronidazole has long carried warnings against alcohol because of a possible disulfiram-like reaction, though researchers have questioned how often that reaction really happens. Our guide to [metronidazole and alcohol](/never-hungover/metronidazole-and-alcohol) walks through what's known. For a broader look at which medicines clash with drinking, see our overview of [alcohol and medications](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications).

**The ALDH2 variant** is the natural version of the same problem. Many people of East Asian descent carry a gene variant that makes their aldehyde dehydrogenase much less active. When they drink, acetaldehyde builds up and they flush, often with a fast heartbeat and nausea. In a sense, eating inky caps temporarily gives anyone a version of that experience. If you flush every time you drink, mushroom or not, our guide to a [red face after drinking](/never-hungover/red-face-after-drinking) explains the causes, and our page on [alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance) covers other reasons drinking can make you feel unwell.

## Why This Matters Even If You Never Forage

The inky cap is a striking real-world demonstration of something that matters for every drinker: **acetaldehyde, not alcohol itself, drives a lot of how bad drinking can make you feel.** When acetaldehyde clears quickly, you notice it less. When it lingers, you get flushing, a pounding heart, nausea, and headache, all of which overlap with how a bad hangover feels.

Researchers still debate exactly how much acetaldehyde contributes to the ordinary next-morning hangover. Dehydration, poor sleep, inflammation, low blood sugar, and congeners (by-products in darker drinks) also play a role. But the inky cap shows clearly that when acetaldehyde builds up, the body reacts strongly and fast. It's also a reminder that a racing heart after drinking isn't always "just the alcohol." If that's something you notice regularly, our article on a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) covers the common causes and when to get checked.

## Common Myths About Inky Caps and Alcohol

**Myth: cooking destroys the toxin.** Coprine isn't broken down by normal cooking, so a cooked inky cap carries the same risk as a raw one.

**Myth: one drink is fine.** Even a single drink can trigger flushing and a racing heart if coprine is active. The reaction tends to scale with how much you drink, but there's no reliably safe amount in the first few days.

**Myth: it's an allergy.** It looks a bit like an allergic reaction because of the flushing, but it isn't one. It's a chemical interaction between the mushroom and alcohol, and it can happen to anyone, the first time they try it.

**Myth: the inky cap is poisonous.** On its own, the common inky cap is considered edible. The problem only arises with alcohol, which is why it's sometimes called "conditionally edible."

**Myth: a supplement can stop the reaction.** There is no good evidence that any supplement, hangover product, or home remedy prevents or reverses a coprine reaction. The only reliable prevention is not drinking during the risk window.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Because this site covers DHM (dihydromyricetin), we want to be clear about this: **DHM is not a fix for an inky cap reaction.** There's no research on DHM and coprine, and you should not drink after eating inky caps on the assumption that any supplement will protect you. If coprine has switched off your aldehyde dehydrogenase, the only safe move is to wait it out.

On a normal night out, the picture is different. DHM is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree, and some animal research suggests it may support the enzymes that break down alcohol and acetaldehyde, with limited human data so far. It isn't a guarantee and doesn't replace drinking less, eating, and hydrating. If you want to try it for ordinary social drinking, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take, and our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers who should check with a doctor first.

## The Bottom Line

The common inky cap is a good meal and a bad drinking companion. A compound in the mushroom, coprine, is converted into a molecule that switches off the enzyme your body uses to clear acetaldehyde. Drink within about three days of eating it, and acetaldehyde builds up fast, bringing flushing, a racing heart, nausea, vomiting, and headache. The reaction usually passes within hours, but it can be dangerous for people with heart problems and can return with every drink.

Keep it simple: skip alcohol for at least 72 hours (five days to be extra safe) after eating inky caps, avoid drinking before the meal, and never combine alcohol with a wild mushroom you haven't eaten before. If you react, stop drinking, lie down, sip water, and call Poison Control. Call 911 for chest pain, fainting, or trouble breathing.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol after eating inky cap mushrooms?**

Not safely, at least not for a few days. The common inky cap (*Coprinopsis atramentaria*) contains coprine, which blocks the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde from alcohol. Drinking within about 72 hours can cause flushing, a racing heart, nausea, vomiting, and headache. Many foragers wait five days to be safe.

**How long after eating inky caps can I drink alcohol?**

Wait at least 72 hours (three days) after your last inky cap meal. Some reports describe reactions a little past three days, so five days is a safer buffer. Also avoid drinking in the hours before the meal, since alcohol still in your system can react once the coprine takes effect.

**What does an inky cap and alcohol reaction feel like?**

It usually starts within minutes to a couple of hours of drinking. The face, neck, and chest turn red and hot, the heart races or pounds, and people often feel nauseated, sweaty, dizzy, and get a throbbing headache. Some notice tingling in the hands or a metallic taste. It usually fades within a few hours but can return with each drink during the risk window.

**Is the inky cap reaction dangerous?**

For most healthy adults it's unpleasant but not life-threatening, and it usually resolves on its own. It can cause low blood pressure, fainting, and strain on the heart, which is riskier for people with heart disease or blood pressure problems. Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) for advice, and call 911 for chest pain, fainting, or trouble breathing.

**Is shaggy mane (shaggy ink cap) safe with alcohol?**

The shaggy mane (*Coprinus comatus*) is generally considered not to contain coprine, and most field guides list it as safe with alcohol. There have been occasional reports of mild symptoms, but there is no good evidence it causes the coprine reaction. The bigger risk is accidentally mixing in common inky caps, so if you're not certain of the species, skip alcohol for three days.

**Does cooking inky caps remove the toxin?**

No. Coprine isn't destroyed by normal cooking, so cooked inky caps can still cause a reaction if you drink. The waiting period is the same no matter how the mushrooms were prepared.

**Why is the inky cap called tippler's bane?**

"Tippler" is an old word for a regular drinker. The nickname comes from the mushroom's well-known habit of making people sick when they drink alcohol after eating it, even though the mushroom is harmless on its own.

**Is the inky cap reaction the same as Antabuse?**

It works in a very similar way. Disulfiram (Antabuse) and the active form of coprine both block aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde builds up when you drink. The symptoms are much the same. The main differences are that disulfiram is a prescription drug whose effect can last up to about two weeks, while the inky cap effect typically lasts around three days.

**Can DHM prevent an inky cap and alcohol reaction?**

There is no good evidence that DHM or any other supplement prevents or reverses a coprine reaction, and you shouldn't rely on one. If you've eaten inky caps, the only reliable way to avoid the reaction is not to drink for at least three days.
